tasks.title: Questions 1–5
tasks.type: YES / NO / NOT GIVEN — do the statements agree with the views of the writer?
tasks.instr: YES — gap yozuvchining fikriga mos; NO — yozuvchining fikriga zid; NOT GIVEN — yozuvchi bu haqda nima deb o'ylashini matndan bilib bo'lmaydi. 1–5 matnning birinchi uch xatboshisiga tegishli.
items: 1 Activities related to environmental protection and space exploration have a common theme.
2 It is unclear why space exploration evolved in a different way from environmental studies on Earth.
3 Governments tend to allocate more money to environmental projects than space exploration.
4 Unfortunately, the environmental and space exploration communities have little to offer each other in terms of resources.
5 The Earth and Space Foundation was set up later than it was originally intended.
why: "Both fields of interest involve what might be referred to as 'scientific exploration'". Common theme = scientific exploration.
"The reason for this dichotomous existence is chiefly historical" — sabab aniq aytilgan (tarixiy va turli mutaxassislar), demak "unclear" ga zid.
Hukumatlar va pul tilga olinadi ("a waste of money, distracting governments"), lekin qaysi sohaga ko'proq mablag' ajratilishi haqida hech narsa yo'q.
"Those involved in space exploration can provide the satellites ... and environmentalists can provide information" — bir-biriga beradigan resurs bor.
Fond tilga olinadi ("was established for the purposes of fostering such links"), lekin qachon va rejadan kechikkani haqida ma'lumot yo'q.
tasks.note: 3- va 5-savollar — Band 7 NOT GIVEN namunasi: gapdagi mavzu matnda bor, lekin gapning ASOSIY da'vosi (more ... than; later than intended) yo'q. 4-savolda "Unfortunately" — baho so'zi; vaziyatning o'zi teskari bo'lgani uchun NO.

tasks.title: Questions 6–9
tasks.type: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D
tasks.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D. Faktik savollar matn tartibida; "writer's purpose" savoli butun matnga tegishli — uni eng oxirida ishlang.
items: 6 What was the significance of the 'novel approach' adopted in the Guatemala project? A) It minimised the need to protect the forests. B) It reduced the impact of tourists on the forests. C) It showed that preserving the forests can be profitable. D) It gave the Foundation greater control over the forests.

7 GPS and satellite imagery were used in the Syrian project to A) help archaeologists find ancient items. B) explore land that is hard to reach. C) reduce the impact of archaeological activity. D) evaluate some early astronomical theories.

8 One of the purposes of the Foundation's awards is to A) attract non-scientists to its work. B) establish priorities for Mars exploration. C) offer financial incentives for space exploration. D) establish the long-term continuity of its activities.

9 What is the writer's purpose in the passage? A) to persuade people to support the Foundation B) to explain the nature of the Foundation's work C) to show how views on the Foundation have changed D) to reject earlier criticisms of the Foundation's work
why: "Another approach is to enhance the value of the forests ... This novel approach is now making the protection of the forests a sensible economic decision." Profitable = sensible economic decision. B — turistlar tilga olinadi, lekin ularning ta'siri kamaygani haqida gap yo'q.

"Used GPS and satellite imagery to locate mounds, or 'tels', containing artefacts and remnants of early civilisations". B — tuzoq: "remote, difficult-to-access Earth locations" boshqa gapda, astronomik kuzatuvlar haqida.

"Together, they demonstrate that the programme really has no boundary ... and they provide longevity for the objectives of the Foundation." Longevity = long-term continuity. C — mukofot pul ekani aytilmagan.
Ohang tushuntiruvchi: Fondning loyihalari birma-bir tasvirlanadi. Yordam so'rash (A), fikrlar o'zgarishi (C) yoki tanqidga javob (D) yo'q.
tasks.note: 6 va 8 — tahliliy savollar: bu matnda isbot xatboshining xulosa (oxirgi) gapida, lekin bu qoida emas — isbot topic gapida ham bo'lishi mumkin, butun xatboshini o'qing. 9 ni eng oxirida ishlang va har noto'g'ri variant uchun "matnda buning isboti qani?" deb so'rang.

tasks.title: Questions 10–14 — Field research: Applying the Earth's environment to the settlement of space
tasks.type: Complete the summary using the words, A–I, below.
tasks.instr: Complete the summary using the words, A–I, below. Javob — HARF. Avval summary qaysi xatboshilarga tegishli ekanini toping, keyin har bo'shliqqa qanday so'z turi kerakligini yozing va qutidagi variantlarni qisqartiring. Summary "Field research also applies..." va "Space-like environments on Earth..." xatboshilariga tegishli.
items: 10 Some studies have looked at how humans function in (10) situations.
11 In one project, it was decided to review cave explorers in Mexico who tolerate (11) periods on their own.
12 It is also possible to prepare for space exploration by studying environments on Earth that are (12) to those on Mars.
13 A huge crater in the Arctic is the (13) place to test the technologies needed to explore Mars ...
14 ... and gather other relevant (14) information.
why: "Physiological and psychological studies in harsh environments". Harsh = extreme.
"The psychology of explorers subjected to long-term isolation in caves in Mexico". Long-term = extended. I (individual) — tuzoq: "on their own" gapda allaqachon bor.

"Space-like environments on Earth help us understand how to operate in the space environment". Space-like = comparable to those on Mars. C (connected) grammatik mos, lekin ma'no — o'xshashlik, bog'liqlik emas.
"The crater ... provides an excellent replica of the physical processes occurring on Mars" — sinov uchun ideal joy.
"How impact craters shape the geological characteristics and possibly biological potential of Mars" — ilmiy ma'lumot. F (beneficial) — matnda asos yo'q.
tasks.note: Ortiqcha variantlar: C connected, E unexpected, F beneficial, I individual. 11-savol — darsning asosiy summary tuzog'i: bo'shliqdan KEYINGI so'zlar (on their own) sizni noto'g'ri variantga yetaklaydi.

tasks.title: Questions 1–5
tasks.type: YES / NO / NOT GIVEN — do the statements agree with the views of the writer?
tasks.instr: YES — gap yozuvchining fikriga mos; NO — yozuvchining fikriga zid; NOT GIVEN — yozuvchi bu haqda nima deb o'ylashini matndan bilib bo'lmaydi.
items: 1 Pictures of Mars suggest it might make a good place for people to settle.
2 Modern Mars and ancient Earth looked remarkably similar.
3 One method of terraforming could involve adapting technology that is already under development.
4 Greenhouse gas factories would provide enough oxygen for people to breathe without special equipment.
5 Terraforming Mars would be an extreme test of human skill and intelligence.
why: "It is just possible that, contrary to photographic evidence, Mars may be more promising than it appears" — suratlar aksincha, Marsni yaroqsiz qilib ko'rsatadi.
Yozuvchi "remarkable parallels between the atmosphere on Earth then and Mars today" deydi — gap atmosfera tarkibi haqida, sayyoralarning TASHQI KO'RINISHI haqida emas.
"With the first already under development, albeit for a different purpose ... With a few changes, it might be possible to use similar mirrors".
"Enough oxygen on the planet for humans to breathe using only special apparatus similar to that used by mountain climbers" — maxsus jihoz baribir kerak.
"It will stretch human ingenuity to its limits". Ingenuity = skill and intelligence.
tasks.note: 2-savol — nozik NOT GIVEN: "remarkable" so'zi matnda bor, lekin "looked" (ko'rinish) emas, "atmosphere" (tarkib). Kalit ham NOT GIVEN.

tasks.title: Questions 6–9
tasks.type: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D
tasks.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D. Faktik savollar matn tartibida; "writer's purpose" savoli butun matnga tegishli — uni eng oxirida ishlang.
items: 6 Which one of these factors suggests that Mars might be a good place for people to settle? A) It is not too far from Earth. B) It has no other life forms living there. C) It has a cool, dry climate. D) It has some similarities with Earth.
7 The first step in terraforming Mars would be to A) make the planet warmer. B) create a breathable atmosphere. C) find a suitable source of water. D) create a habitat for living organisms.

8 Special factories on Mars could be used to A) control the level of greenhouse gases. B) absorb excess levels of carbon dioxide. C) produce oxygen in a manner similar to plants. D) help grow essential bacteria.

9 What is the writer's main purpose in the passage? A) To explain why we need to terraform Mars. B) To illustrate the three processes required to terraform a planet like Mars. C) To consider how and why Mars might be terraformed. D) To demonstrate how straightforward it would be to terraform a planet.
why: "It does have some things in common with our own planet" — aylanish tezligi, o'q og'ishi, hayot uchun kerakli elementlar. A — teskari: "a very distant place"; C — "viciously cold, dry" salbiy omil.
"Would initially create a greenhouse effect that would heat the planet"; "Martian global warming, the first stage".
"The same factories would then produce oxygen by mimicking the natural process of plant photosynthesis". A — tuzoq: zavodlar gazlarni nazorat qilmaydi, balki chiqaradi.

Matn ham "why" (aholi o'sishi, insoniyat omon qolishi), ham "how" (uch usul) ni ko'rib chiqadi. B — "three processes REQUIRED" noto'g'ri: bular uch muqobil usul; D — yozuvchi "neither cheap nor easy" deydi.
tasks.note: 9-savolda B eng xavfli tuzoq: matnda haqiqatan uchta usul bor, lekin ular BIRGALIKDA kerakli bosqichlar emas, balki TAKLIF qilingan muqobillar ("Three terraforming methods have been suggested").

tasks.title: Questions 10–14
tasks.type: Complete the summary using a word A–I from the box.
tasks.instr: Qutida faqat FE'LLAR. Javob — HARF. Avval summary qaysi xatboshilarga tegishli ekanini toping, keyin har bo'shliqqa qanday so'z turi kerakligini yozing va qutidagi variantlarni qisqartiring. Summary uchinchi usulga (Zubrin va McKay, asteroidlar) tegishli.
items: 10 One method of terraforming Mars would be to (10) asteroids at the planet.
11 Rockets attached to an enormous asteroid would propel it towards Mars, taking ten years to (11) the enormous distances required.
12 The asteroid would (12) the planet with incredible force ...
13 ... and (13) enough energy ...
14 ... to (14) the planet's temperature.
why: "By firing large, ammonia-bearing asteroids at the planet". Fire at = shoot at.
"It would take each asteroid about ten years to reach its destination". "Cover a distance" — tayyor kollokatsiya.
"One asteroid slamming into Mars' surface". Slam into = hit (with incredible force). E (land) — "land the planet" grammatik emas.
"The energy produced by one asteroid" — energiya hosil qilish = create. G (power) — ot/fe'l, lekin "power enough energy" kollokatsiya emas.
"Would raise the temperature of the planet by three degrees". Raise = increase. H (rise) — o'timsiz fe'l, to'ldiruvchi bilan ishlatilmaydi.
tasks.note: Ortiqcha variantlar: E land, F drive, G power, H rise. 14-savolni grammatika bilan tushuntiring: "the temperature rises" (o'timsiz), "they increase / raise the temperature" (o'timli).

readings.title: Practice 1: The junkyard above our heads
readings.qtype: Yes/No/Not Given (1–5) + Multiple choice A–D (6–9) + Summary, word box A–I (10–14)
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn (Passage 3 darajasi, Band 7)
text: Since the first artificial satellite was launched in 1957, humanity has placed many thousands of objects in orbit around the Earth. Some of them are still doing useful work, but a far larger number are not. Dead satellites, discarded rocket stages, lost tools and the fragments left by collisions and explosions now circle the planet alongside the working spacecraft on which we depend. Space agencies track more than 30,000 pieces larger than about ten centimetres, and statistical models suggest that there are around a million pieces larger than one centimetre and many millions smaller than that. It is, in my view, one of the most underestimated environmental problems of our age, largely because it happens out of sight.

The size of a fragment matters far less than one might expect. In low orbit, objects travel at around 28,000 kilometres per hour, so even a fleck of paint can strike with the force of a bullet. The windows of the Space Shuttle had to be replaced after many missions because of damage from tiny particles, and the International Space Station regularly adjusts its orbit to avoid larger pieces. Its crew have, on several occasions, had to shelter in their return capsules while a fragment passed close by.

The greater danger, however, is not the loss of a single spacecraft. In 1978, the NASA scientist Donald Kessler described what might happen if the number of objects in a particular orbit passed a critical level: each collision would produce fragments that caused further collisions, until the orbit became unusable for generations. Some commentators still treat this scenario as science fiction. I find such complacency difficult to understand. In 2009, a working communications satellite collided with a defunct Russian satellite, producing well over a thousand trackable fragments, and several weapons tests in which countries deliberately destroyed their own satellites have added thousands more. Neither kind of event has yet started a runaway chain reaction, but both show that the process Kessler described is a physical reality rather than a theoretical curiosity.

Why should any of this concern people on the ground? The answer is that modern life depends on satellites far more than most of us realise. Weather forecasting, navigation, the timing signals that allow banks to process transactions, and the monitoring of crops, forests and ice sheets all rely on spacecraft in orbit. It is sometimes argued that money spent on cleaning up space would be better spent on environmental problems here on Earth. This argument seems to me to misunderstand the situation entirely, since much of our knowledge of those problems comes from the very satellites that debris threatens.

What is being done? For many years, international guidelines have recommended that operators remove satellites from low orbit within 25 years of the end of their mission, either by lowering them so that they burn up in the atmosphere or by moving them to a little-used 'graveyard' orbit. Yet these guidelines are voluntary, and compliance has been patchy: a significant proportion of satellites have simply been left where they failed. Some national regulators have recently shortened the period to five years, a welcome step, although it applies only to the satellites they license.

Engineers, meanwhile, have designed a variety of ways of capturing debris, including nets, harpoons, magnetic plates and robotic arms, and several of these have been tested in orbit with encouraging results. However, the costs remain high, and no company has yet removed a large piece of debris on a commercial basis. There is also a legal difficulty: under international law, a dead satellite remains the property of the state that launched it, so another country or company cannot simply remove it without permission.

For these reasons, I do not believe that technology alone will solve the problem. What is needed above all is a binding international agreement, perhaps based on the principle that those who create debris should pay for its removal. Such an agreement will not be easy to reach, but the alternative is to allow the space around our planet to become as polluted as some of its oceans.

readings.title: Practice 2: Why go back to the Moon?
readings.qtype: Yes/No/Not Given (1–5) + Multiple choice A–D (6–9) + Summary, word box A–I (10–14)
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn (Passage 3 darajasi, Band 7)
text: When the last Apollo astronauts left the Moon in December 1972, few people would have predicted that more than half a century would pass before anyone attempted to return. Yet that is exactly what happened. It is often forgotten that Apollo was, above all, a political project: its purpose was to demonstrate American superiority during the Cold War, and science was a secondary concern. Once the race had been won, the political motivation disappeared, public interest faded, and budgets were cut. The remaining missions were cancelled, and attention turned to space stations in low Earth orbit.

Today, however, the Moon is once again a destination. The United States, China, India, Japan and the European Space Agency all have lunar programmes, and a number of private companies are building landers of their own. Critics ask why, having already been there, we should go back at all. It is a reasonable question, but I believe the answer is that we will not be doing the same thing again. The Apollo astronauts spent, at most, three days on the surface, close to the equator. The new missions aim to stay much longer and to explore regions that no human has ever seen.

The most important of these regions is the area around the south pole. Several spacecraft have found strong evidence that water ice exists inside deep craters there which never receive sunlight, where temperatures fall below minus 200 degrees Celsius. The significance of this can hardly be overstated. Water is extremely heavy and therefore expensive to launch from Earth; ice found on the Moon could provide drinking water for astronauts and, once split into hydrogen and oxygen, rocket fuel. A base near the south pole could therefore become a kind of filling station for missions travelling further into the solar system.

The Moon is also of great value to science in its own right. Because it has no atmosphere, wind or rain, its surface preserves a record of the early solar system that has long been erased on Earth. The far side, which always faces away from our planet, is especially promising. Shielded from the radio noise produced by human activity, it may be the quietest place in our neighbourhood for radio astronomy, and astronomers have long argued that a telescope there could detect faint signals from the early universe that cannot be picked up from Earth.

The role of private companies is perhaps the most striking difference from the Apollo era. Instead of designing and operating every spacecraft themselves, space agencies now increasingly buy transport services from commercial firms. The early results have been mixed: several privately built landers have crashed or tipped over on landing. Some observers have taken these failures as proof that the Moon should be left to experienced government agencies. I see them rather differently. Every successful space programme, including Apollo, experienced failures in its early years, and competition between companies seems likely to reduce costs in the long run.

None of this means that a return to the Moon is free of difficulties. Lunar dust is a particular problem. Because there is no wind or water to wear the particles down, they remain sharp and jagged, like tiny pieces of broken glass. The Apollo astronauts found that the dust clung to their suits, damaged seals on their equipment and irritated their eyes and lungs. On a long stay, such problems would become far more serious. Radiation, too, is a constant threat, since the Moon has neither a thick atmosphere nor a magnetic field to protect those on its surface.

There is also the question of lunar tourism, which some companies are already advertising. Personally, I would be in no hurry to see it. The Moon's surface has remained almost untouched for billions of years, and the footprints and equipment left by the Apollo crews are now historical sites. Before large numbers of visitors arrive, we need clear international rules on how these places will be protected. The Moon belongs to no one, and that is precisely why it deserves careful treatment.

readings.title: Practice 3 (uyga): Is anyone out there?
readings.qtype: Yes/No/Not Given (1–5) + Multiple choice A–D (6–9) + Summary, word box A–I (10–14)
readings.source: Jony Academy — yangi matn (Passage 3 darajasi, Band 7), uy vazifasi
text: In April 1960, a young astronomer named Frank Drake used a radio telescope at Green Bank, West Virginia, to listen to two nearby stars similar to the Sun, hoping to detect signals that nature could not have produced. He heard nothing of interest, but his modest experiment, known as Project Ozma, began a search that has continued, on and off, for more than sixty years. The search for extraterrestrial intelligence, usually shortened to SETI, has still not detected a single confirmed signal, and some people conclude from this that the whole enterprise has been a failure. I would argue the opposite: we have barely begun to look.

The scale of the task is easy to underestimate. Our galaxy alone contains somewhere between one hundred and four hundred billion stars, and since the 1990s astronomers have confirmed the existence of more than five thousand planets orbiting stars other than the Sun. Data from space telescopes suggest that a significant proportion of Sun-like stars have rocky planets at a distance where liquid water could exist. A signal from any one of them might be faint, brief, or broadcast at a frequency that no one has thought to monitor. One researcher has compared the searching done so far to scooping a single glass of water from the ocean and concluding that the ocean contains no fish.

The search has also had to survive long periods without public money. In 1992, NASA launched an ambitious survey of the sky that was intended to last ten years, but within about a year Congress had cancelled its funding, partly because critics dismissed the project as a waste of taxpayers' money. Since then, most SETI research has depended on private donors. The SETI Institute, a non-profit organisation founded in 1984, has kept the work going, and in 2015 the Breakthrough Listen project was launched with a promise of 100 million dollars over ten years. In my view, the withdrawal of public funding was short-sighted: the instruments and software developed for SETI have produced valuable data for ordinary astronomy, and a confirmed signal would rank among the most important discoveries in human history.

The most famous candidate signal so far shows how difficult the work can be. On 15 August 1977, the Big Ear radio telescope at Ohio State University recorded a burst of radio energy that was far stronger than the background noise and confined to a very narrow range of frequencies. When the astronomer Jerry Ehman noticed it on a computer printout a few days later, he circled the readings and wrote 'Wow!' in the margin. The signal had exactly the characteristics expected of an artificial transmission, but it was never detected again, despite many later attempts to find it. Various natural explanations have since been proposed, and none has been generally accepted. Without repetition, a single signal, however striking, cannot count as evidence.

Modern technology has transformed the search. Where Drake's receiver could monitor only a single radio channel, today's equipment can analyse billions of channels simultaneously, and between 1999 and 2020 millions of volunteers lent the spare processing power of their home computers to a project called SETI@home. Researchers are also looking beyond radio: they search for brief pulses of laser light and for gases in the atmospheres of distant planets that, on Earth, are produced mainly by industry. Ironically, technology has also made the work harder. The radio spectrum is now so crowded with signals from mobile phones and satellites that separating a genuine transmission from human interference has become one of the main problems facing the field.

A more controversial question is whether we should only listen or also transmit. In 1974, astronomers used the giant Arecibo telescope in Puerto Rico to send a short coded message towards a star cluster some 25,000 light years away, and several private groups have since beamed messages at nearby stars. Supporters argue that if every civilisation only listens, no one will ever hear anything. The physicist Stephen Hawking, however, warned that announcing our presence could be dangerous, since a more advanced civilisation might not be friendly. On this point I share his caution. A message, once sent, cannot be recalled, and no individual or organisation has the right to speak for the whole of humanity without wider agreement.

Even if no signal is ever found, I do not believe the search will have been wasted. It has encouraged people to think about how life begins, how long civilisations survive and what our own planet might look like to a distant observer. The physicist Enrico Fermi is said to have asked his colleagues over lunch in 1950, 'Where is everybody?' More than seventy years later, we still do not know the answer. But a silence that has been carefully measured tells us something too, and the only way to measure it is to keep listening.

tasks.title: Questions 1–5
tasks.type: YES / NO / NOT GIVEN — do the statements agree with the views of the writer?
tasks.instr: YES — gap yozuvchining fikriga mos; NO — yozuvchining fikriga zid; NOT GIVEN — yozuvchi bu haqda nima deb o'ylashini matndan bilib bo'lmaydi. 5 daqiqa.
items: 1 The lack of a confirmed signal shows that SETI has been a failure.
2 People often fail to appreciate how large the task facing SETI is.
3 A single striking signal can be regarded as evidence of alien intelligence.
4 Messages should not be sent into space without wider agreement.
5 Enrico Fermi was convinced that there were no other civilisations.
why: "Some people conclude from this that the whole enterprise has been a failure. I would argue the opposite: we have barely begun to look." — yozuvchi bu xulosaga qarshi.
"The scale of the task is easy to underestimate." Fail to appreciate how large = underestimate the scale.
"Without repetition, a single signal, however striking, cannot count as evidence." Gap matnga to'g'ridan-to'g'ri zid.
"No individual or organisation has the right to speak for the whole of humanity without wider agreement." Yozuvchi o'zi aytadi: "On this point I share his caution."
Fermi faqat savol bergan ("Where is everybody?"); uning o'zi nimaga ishongani matnda aytilmagan. Kalit so'z bor, da'vo yo'q — NOT GIVEN.

tasks.title: Questions 6–9
tasks.type: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D
tasks.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D. Faktik savollar matn tartibida; "writer's purpose" savoli butun matnga tegishli — uni eng oxirida ishlang.
items: 6 What is the writer's opinion of the decision to stop funding NASA's survey? A) It was justified because the survey had found nothing. B) It was unwise because SETI also helps ordinary astronomy. C) It forced scientists to give up searching for signals. D) It made little difference to the progress of the search.

7 What does the writer say about the 'Wow!' signal? A) It was later shown to come from a comet. B) It was detected again by other telescopes. C) It has never been satisfactorily explained. D) It was recorded by a telescope in Puerto Rico.

8 Why does the writer mention Stephen Hawking? A) to introduce a concern that the writer shares B) to support the idea of sending more messages C) to explain how the Arecibo message was designed D) to show that physicists disagree with astronomers

9 What is the writer's main purpose in the passage? A) to describe the history of radio astronomy B) to explain why no signals have been detected so far C) to compare government and private approaches to SETI D) to argue that the search is worth continuing
why: "In my view, the withdrawal of public funding was short-sighted: the instruments and software developed for SETI have produced valuable data for ordinary astronomy". Short-sighted = unwise. A — tanqidchilarning fikri (waste of money), yozuvchiniki emas; C — ish xususiy mablag' bilan davom etgan ("has kept the work going"); D — matnda asos yo'q: aksincha, izlash "had to survive long periods without public money".

"Various natural explanations have since been proposed, and none has been generally accepted." B — teskari: "never detected again"; D — tuzoq: Puerto Rico (Arecibo) 6-xatboshida, signal esa Ohio'da qayd etilgan; A — kometa matnda tilga olinmaydi, tabiiy izohlarning hech biri qabul qilinmagan ("shown" noto'g'ri).

"The physicist Stephen Hawking, however, warned that announcing our presence could be dangerous ... On this point I share his caution." B — teskari: Hawking xabar yuborishdan ogohlantirgan; C — Arecibo xabarining tuzilishi haqida gap yo'q; D — umumlashtirish: fiziklar va astronomlar guruh sifatida solishtirilmaydi.

Yozuvchi "SETI muvaffaqiyatsiz" degan fikrni rad etadi (1-xatboshi), moliyalashni to'xtatishni tanqid qiladi va "the only way to measure it is to keep listening" deb yakunlaydi — bu dalilli bahs: izlashni davom ettirishga arziydi. B — sabablar (vazifa ko'lami) bahsning bir qismi xolos; C — davlat va xususiy mablag' faqat bitta xatboshida; A — tarixiy faktlar (1960, 1977) faqat misol sifatida keltirilgan.

tasks.title: Questions 10–14 — New tools, new problems
tasks.type: Complete the summary using the words, A–I, below.
tasks.instr: Complete the summary using the words, A–I, below. Javob — HARF. Avval summary qaysi xatboshilarga tegishli ekanini toping, keyin har bo'shliqqa qanday so'z turi kerakligini yozing va qutidagi variantlarni qisqartiring. Summary bitta xatboshiga (zamonaviy texnologiya: imkoniyat va muammo) tegishli.
items: 10 Drake's receiver could monitor just one channel, but today's equipment is far more (10).
11 Between 1999 and 2020, millions of ordinary people (11) the unused power of their home computers to SETI@home.
12 Researchers are no longer (12) to radio: they also look for brief flashes of laser light ...
13 ... and for gases in planetary atmospheres that, on Earth, mostly come from (13) activity.
14 However, crowded radio frequencies have made it harder to (14) real signals from human interference.
why: "Today's equipment can analyse billions of channels simultaneously" — bitta kanal o'rniga milliardlab: far more powerful. C (expensive) — narx haqida matnda gap yo'q; G (restricted) — teskari ma'no.
"Millions of volunteers lent the spare processing power of their home computers". Lent = offered (ko'ngilli ravishda berdi). H (sold) — grammatik mos, lekin ko'ngillilar sotmagan.
"Researchers are also looking beyond radio" — endi faqat radio bilan cheklanmagan: no longer restricted to radio. "Restricted to" — tayyor birikma (sifatdosh + to).
"Gases ... that, on Earth, are produced mainly by industry" → industrial activity. I (volcanic) — tuzoq: tabiiy manba, matnda esa sanoat.

"Separating a genuine transmission from human interference" → distinguish ... from. A (block) grammatik mos ko'rinadi, lekin ma'no teskari: maqsad haqiqiy signalni to'sish emas, uni xalaqitdan ajratish.
tasks.note: Ortiqcha variantlar: A block, C expensive, H sold, I volcanic. 13-savol — Band 7 tuzog'i: ikkala sifat ham (industrial / volcanic) "activity" bilan birikadi, faqat matn hal qiladi.

homework_intro: Bugun Passage 3 da uch savol turini birga ishladik: xarita → YNNG (yozuvchi fikri) → MCQ (faktik va tahliliy) → summary qutisi → oxirida writer's purpose. Uyda xuddi shu tartibda, 20 daqiqa ichida ishlaysiz.

Birinchi vazifa — Practice 3 "Is anyone out there?": 20 daqiqa vaqt oling va 14 savolga javob bering. Har YNNG javobi yoniga isbot gapning birinchi uch so'zini yozing; summary uchun har bo'shliq yoniga so'z turini yozing (ot / fe'l / sifat).

Ikkinchi vazifa — Student's Book, 88-bet, Vocabulary 1–2-mashqlar ("Verbs and dependent prepositions"): SB matnidagi fe'l + predlog birikmalari (focus on, referred to as, reflected in, regarded as, distract from, stem from, result from). Har birikma bilan koinot haqida bitta o'z gapingizni ham yozing.

Uchinchi vazifa — xatolar daftari: bugungi (SB, WB, Practice 1–2) xato javoblarni yozing — savol, to'g'ri javob va sabab ("NO va NOT GIVEN ni adashtirdim", "qutidagi so'z turi mos emas edi", "purpose savolida bitta xatboshiga qaradim" va h.k.).

homework.title: Practice 3: "Is anyone out there?"
homework.instr: 20 daqiqada 14 savol; YNNG uchun isbot gap, summary uchun so'z turi yoziladi.
homework.answers: Javoblar Reading bo'limida izoh bilan.

homework.title: Student's Book, 88-bet: Vocabulary 1–2-mashq
homework.instr: Fe'l + predlog (1-mashq: 6 ta parcha, 2-mashq: 7 ta gap) + har birikma bilan o'z gapingiz.
homework.answers: 1-mashq: 1 on 2 as 3 in 4 as; from 5 from 6 from. 2-mashq: 1 in; on 2 to 3 with 4 from 5 in 6 to 7 as.

homework.title: Xatolar daftari
homework.instr: Bugungi xato javoblar: savol — to'g'ri javob — xato sababi.
homework.answers: Sababsiz qator qabul qilinmaydi.

kahoot.q: In YES/NO/NOT GIVEN, what are you checking?
options: General facts that you already know
Only the numbers and dates in the text
Your own opinion on the topic
kahoot.explain: YNNG — yozuvchi fikri va da'vosi. O'z bilimingiz yoki fikringiz hisobga olinmaydi.

kahoot.q: Text: 'The reason for this split is chiefly historical.' Statement: 'It is unclear why the split exists.'
kahoot.explain: Sabab aniq aytilgan (historical) — "unclear" ga zid. Demak NO.

kahoot.q: Text mentions governments and money. Statement: 'Governments give more money to X than Y.' No comparison exists.
kahoot.explain: Mavzu bor, lekin taqqoslash (more ... than) yo'q — NOT GIVEN.

kahoot.q: What is the difference between NO and NOT GIVEN?
options: NO = text says the opposite; NG = no information
NO = no information; NG = text says the opposite
They mean the same: the statement is not true
NG is only for numbers and dates; NO is for ideas
kahoot.explain: NO — matnda zid ma'lumot bor. NOT GIVEN — yozuvchining bu haqdagi fikri umuman yo'q.

kahoot.q: Where can the answer to a 'significance' or 'purpose' MCQ be found?
options: In the topic or concluding sentence — check both
Always in the very last sentence of the paragraph
Only in the title and subheadings of the text
Only in the opening sentence of the passage
kahoot.explain: Xatboshi vazifasi topic gapda ham, xulosa gapda ham bo'lishi mumkin — butun xatboshini o'qing. SB 6 da isbot oxirgi gapda ("This novel approach is now making ... a sensible economic decision"), lekin bu qoida emas.

kahoot.q: When should you answer 'What is the writer's purpose in the passage?'
options: Last, after reading the whole passage
First, before reading any of the passage
Only if time is left after checking
kahoot.explain: Purpose butun matnga tegishli — ohangni aniqlash uchun matnni o'qib bo'lgach ishlang.

kahoot.q: A text describes projects with examples, no requests or criticisms. The writer's purpose is to…
kahoot.explain: Chaqiriq yo'q (persuade emas), tanqid yo'q, vaqt bo'yicha o'zgarish yo'q — tushuntirish (SB 9 = B).

kahoot.q: Summary with a word box: what do you write on the answer sheet?
kahoot.explain: Quti berilgan bo'lsa — faqat HARF. So'z yozsangiz 0 ball.

kahoot.q: 'who tolerate ___ periods on their own' — which option fits best?
kahoot.explain: "Long-term isolation" = extended periods. "Individual" — tuzoq: "on their own" gapda allaqachon bor.

kahoot.q: 'environments that are ___ to those on Mars' — which words fit grammatically?
kahoot.explain: "___ to" — comparable to, connected to. Ma'no bo'yicha comparable (space-like environments).

kahoot.q: 'enough energy to ___ the planet's temperature' — why is 'rise' wrong?
options: 'Rise' can only be used as a noun
'Rise' is too informal for academic texts
kahoot.explain: Rise — o'timsiz fe'l (the temperature rises). To'ldiruvchi bilan o'timli fe'l kerak: increase.

kahoot.q: An MCQ option repeats words from the text, but the text says 'Neither event has yet started a chain reaction'. It is…
options: a trap — the text denies it
correct — it uses the same words
kahoot.explain: So'zlar bir xil, ma'no teskari. Passage 3 da eng ko'p uchraydigan MCQ tuzog'i.

kahoot.q: Both Earth and space exploration ___ from the same human curiosity.
kahoot.explain: Stem from — ... dan kelib chiqmoq. Focus on, refer to, allocate to — boshqa predlog va ma'no.

kahoot.q: The Arctic crater is an excellent ___ of conditions on Mars.
kahoot.explain: Replica — aynan o'xshash nusxa. Remnant/artefact — qadimiy qoldiq va buyum.

kahoot.q: The charity was established to ___ links between the two communities.
kahoot.explain: Foster links — aloqalarni rivojlantirmoq. Divert/distract — chalg'itmoq.

kahoot.q: The awards provide ___ for the Foundation's objectives.
kahoot.explain: Longevity — uzoq davom etish. Shuning uchun Q8 javobi D: long-term continuity.

kahoot.q: Terraforming would stretch human ___ to its limits.
kahoot.explain: Ingenuity — zukkolik, ixtirochilik = skill and intelligence (WB 5-savol, YES).

kahoot.q: The challenge of making Mars habitable is ___ with difficulties.
kahoot.explain: Be fraught with — xavf yoki qiyinchilikka to'la. "Full of" dan keyin "with" kelmaydi; prone va susceptible esa "to" bilan ishlatiladi (prone to, susceptible to).

kahoot.q: Which word means 'able to support life'?
kahoot.explain: Habitable — yashashga yaroqli. Barren — hosilsiz, cho'l; remote — uzoq.

kahoot.q: Guidelines are ___, so many operators simply ignore them.
kahoot.explain: Voluntary — ixtiyoriy; shuning uchun e'tiborsiz qoldiriladi. Binding/compulsory — majburiy.

lessons.title: Unit 8 Listening — Section 4: Note completion (lecture)
lessons.grammar_topic: Section 4 (akademik ma'ruza): Note completion — sarlavhali konspekt, 10 bo'shliq pauzasiz, NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS; bo'shliqni bashorat qilish, signpost iboralar, paraphrase va tuzoqlar (Band 7)
lessons.vocab_topic: Unit 8 (Across the universe) — astronomiya, teleskoplar, havaskor kuzatuvchilar, kosmosda inson salomatligi
lessons.book_ref: Complete IELTS Bands 6.5–7.5: Student's Book, Unit 8, 88–89-betlar (Listening Section 4, CD2 Track 17; skript — 159–160-betlar); Workbook, Unit 8, 50–51-betlar (Listening Section 4, Track 13; skript — 61-bet).
objectives: Section 4 konspektining tuzilishini (sarlavhalar, kichik sarlavhalar, belgilar) ma'ruza rejasi sifatida o'qish va har bo'limda qaysi savollar kelishini oldindan bilish.
Har bo'shliq uchun so'z turi va ma'no toifasini bashorat qilish: grammatik belgilar (an ___ → unli bilan boshlanadigan ot; ___ observations → sifat), kollokatsiyalar (research ___, accurate ___).
Ma'ruzachining signpost iboralaridan (So let's have a look at..., Firstly..., Secondly..., The biggest problem, though...) konspektdagi joyni kuzatish.
Paraphrase va tuzoqlarni tanish: kutilgan javob rad etilishi (don't care if ... beautiful → research data), bir xil mavzudagi ikki misol (solar eclipse / the Moon with a plane).
Transfer qoidalari: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS, imlo, ko'plik, qavsdagi ixtiyoriy so'zlar (the) Earth, (bone) fractures.

Kolonka yoki quloqchin; Kahoot (20 savol) — dars oxirida.
